371.s: Jones values Steinway's action and tone over Yamaha and other makes.

371.t: Piano personalities and choosing matched pianos with John Lewis
371.s: Every piano sounds different; Jones and John Lewis tried 50 Steinways to find two that matched for their duo record.
371.q: If they are I haven't noticed. I have always felt that Steinway's had the most even sound of all of the pianos. It seems that some of the other pianos, I won't mention any names, but they seemed to lose their tonality in the higher that you get in the higher registers. Sometimes, the lower…

371.t: Attachment to Steinways from JATP and contract requirements
371.s: The JATP tours made him a Steinway player; his contract asks only for a tuned, regulated piano.

118.t: Baby Bruce, the party pianist, and the damp-proof piano
118.s: Russell and Williams talk about interviewing Baby Bruce and his waterlogged piano, then discuss Williams's own damp-proof piano.
118.q: You know you wouldn't believe when they got some of these fellas around him singing and playing a little piano. I think if the people could hear him they'd get a break.

303.t: Selling pianos and player pianos at Werlein's

303.q: I have been on and off at Whirlions since 1926. That's before my time. Ted Frank I knew when he was four years old. Ted was four when I first went to work at Whirlions. Ted's been very very sick but he's recovering. Ted had a terrible heart condition. He lost oh some 40-50 pounds.

349.t: Playing at the White House and the Bosendorfer pianos
349.s: With Hampton he played for several presidents, enjoying Bosendorfer pianos.
349.q: Oh yes, yes. The piano, one, in fact twice, Bosendorfer pianos. Oh. Boy what a keyboard. I’ll never forget — I sure would have loved to have one of them pianos.

722.s: Talk about his drafting-style workspace and an upright Steinway from Eastman's first delivery in 1921.

512.s: Both recall the suitcase Rhodes, its better sound and the hassle of moving it, including Zawinul and Cannonball.
512.q: Oh people don’t know, that was a trip. But that one had the better sound.

528.s: Tyner explains why he values Steinway and its artist program.
528.ch: Steinway, Blue Note, awards and wrap-up
528.q: Well they make one of the greatest pianos in the world. The way it’s constructed, the way it sounds, they really know what they’re doing and they have had years and years of opportunities to perfect the instrument. Steinway is a really great piano and it’s durability, the fact that you can play it…

383.s: Wilson prefers a nine-foot German Steinway for its response and reward for effort over louder-sounding pianos.
383.q: And some Baldwins, they're loud, and they're not loud enough, and you know they're too loud, and yet you feel like hitting them harder and harder and it's loud, but see, it don't feel loud. But it sounds loud. Yet, a Steinway feels loud when you hit it, and it is loud, too.

148.t: Out-of-tune pianos, the Rhodes and the Yamaha electric piano
148.s: Pianos are poorly kept; he finds the Rhodes decent and a Yamaha closest to acoustic.
148.q: Yeah; right, that's happened a lot of times. Pianos aren't cared for very well in this country. In most commercial places they don't keep them up, they don't have them tuned, they let them go down and they go down and down.

412.s: When Earl Hines replaced Scobey, the manager spent $4100 a week on music but bought a $150 piano and painted it black.
412.q: And it was ridiculous and I couldn't cure it. Well, finally, the Continental -- Bob did leave for a stretch and they put Earl Hines in. And now, there's a story I want to tell about that. Earl Hines is coming in, we got to get a piano. They had an upright Kimball and it was a gas but now we got to…

81.t: His piano bought on 125th Street in 1928 and its tuner
81.s: He rented then bought a piano in 1928; a Black tuner spent whole days voicing it so it sounded like velvet.
81.q: Well, I intend to get down there and see what condition it is in soon, and if it's in nice condition, well, then, who knows -- I may knock off one for this particular thing.

13.t: The Grand Terrace room and its piano
13.s: The club was redone in silver; Wilson recalls the huge German grand.
13.ch: Joining Earl Hines and the Grand Terrace
13.q: Yeah, well, at first it was just like the old style cabaret, you know, a lot of drapes and things around there. And then they remodeled, and modernized the joint. So then it was did out in beautiful silver, new band-stand, everything. But it was a beautiful place.
